title: The Fastest Way to Feel Valuable Again
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder's short essay makes one substantive claim and pursues it: the opposite of anxiety is not calm but purpose, and purpose is felt through service rather than worked out in advance. She reports seeing this most clearly in younger people, whose fog and anxiety lift the moment they feel useful, and draws the distinction that they do not need to know their purpose, only to feel their impact. The definitional move at the centre of the piece is that purpose is not the thing you do but what happens in others when you do it. From there she strips away the prerequisites people invent for feeling valuable, the business plan, the audience, the title, the website and even clarity itself, leaving only usefulness. Her own recent experience supports the point: rooms where she was solving the right problems rather than performing or proving produced visible evidence in unexpected thank-you messages and in other people stepping up. The prescription is a reframe rather than a programme, do something valuable rather than waiting to feel valuable, on the understanding that purpose reveals itself in the process of creating impact.
points: The reframe that purpose is not the thing you do but what happens in others when you do it relocates purpose from self-examination to observable effect.
Mulder inverts the usual sequence of clarity then action, arguing that impact comes first and purpose is revealed by it rather than preceding it.
Her evidence for the claim is deliberately small-scale: thank-you texts, an email saying that helped, someone else stepping up in their own work.
Positioning purpose rather than calm as anxiety's opposite implies that stuckness is better treated with usefulness than with rest or breathing techniques.
She notes the shift in her own working life came from being in rooms where she solved rather than performed, tying the argument back to alignment rather than visibility.
quotes: And more often than not, you don’t find that purpose by figuring it out. You feel it by being of service.
That sense of depression, fog, anxiety… it lifts the moment they feel useful. Not when they know their purpose, but when they feel their impact.
Most people confuse purpose with “the thing they’re supposed to do.” But purpose isn’t the thing you do. It’s what happens in others when you do what you do.
It’s the relief, insight, clarity, or hope someone else feels because you showed up and did your thing.
Don’t wait to feel valuable. Do something valuable. Service is the fastest way home.
You just have to create impact (even in the smallest of gestures), and the purpose will reveal itself in the process.
